tecnicas.observacao: Prompt base de instrução direta: «Generate secure Python code for the following: <coding task>». O requisito «secure» foi classificado como restrição de segurança em linguagem natural. A tarefa (trecho de código incompleto com docstring) é o próprio enunciado e está em todas as condições; não foi classificada como contexto adicional. Condição de referência, sem contrafactual próprio.

tecnicas.observacao: Três passos (gerar, revisar procurando problemas de segurança, melhorar com base na crítica), com duas iterações do laço crítica-melhoria. O passo 1 é idêntico ao prompt baseline, de modo que a Tabela II contém a condição com e sem o laço de autocrítica (baseline vs. RCI) nos mesmos modelos e tarefas. É o comparador da RQ1 (técnica de referência da literatura, adotada de [7] e [2]); o isolamento é do pacote de autocrítica com duas iterações, não de um passo individual.

tecnicas.observacao: O prompt baseline recebe, anexadas, as 10 diretrizes de codificação segura mais similares (pares precondição-diretriz) recuperadas da base SecGuide (320 entradas derivadas de CWE/MITRE e recomendações do CodeQL) por similaridade de cosseno entre embeddings (text-embedding-3-small, ChromaDB). O acréscimo é um bloco único que combina conhecimento externo recuperado (contexto) e regras de segurança a seguir (restricoes; essa categoria já estava presente no baseline, em forma mais fraca, pelo termo «secure»). As diretrizes não são exemplos resolvidos. Baseline e RAG diferem apenas nesse bloco (Tabela I), mas o contrafactual é do pacote recuperação + diretrizes; não autoriza atribuir o ganho a um só mecanismo.

Validação manual seguindo critérios definidos em [2] para reduzir viés humano.

citacoes.trecho: In this work, we investigate the effect of incorporating secure coding guidelines, relevant to a given coding task, on the security of code generated by LLMs.
Here, the LLM was prompted to generate secure Python code for a given task without any additional security-related information.
Here, the model was first prompted to generate a secure Python implementation.
Lastly, based on this feedback, the model was prompted to refine its initial response to enhance the security of the code.
For our experiments, we performed two iterations of the feedback-improvement loop [2].
Once the relevant guidelines were retrieved, they were appended to the coding task and supplied to the LLM for code generation.
In our experiments, we retrieved the top 10 relevant guidelines per task (see Section III-C).
To address RQ2, we used the RCI+RAG as the fourth approach where we combined RCI and RAG by appending the relevant guidelines to the initial prompt used in the RCI process.
To ensure maximum reproducibility, we set the temperature to 0.0 [2] and the top_p to 0.1 [2] across all models.
However, RCI relies on the model’s ability to identify security flaws, which is constrained by its training data and susceptibility to hallucinations.
However, for CWE-78 (‘OS Command Injection’) and CWE-502 (‘Deserialization of Untrusted Data’), RAG resulted in a slight increase in detected weaknesses across all three models.

This problem may stem from RCI’s iterative three-step process (with two iterations in our setup), where the model refines its response at each step, potentially causing the code to drift from the initial task, compared to RAG’s direct single-step prompting.
Similar to RCI, RCI+RAG also resulted in fewer valid code snippets with respect to baseline and RAG.
However, the potential for direct contamination existed due to the publication of the SecurityEval dataset two years prior to this study.
We conducted a basic contamination test on the results of the main experiment using the Dolos toolkit [41] to quantify the impact of any potential leakage.
As this study exclusively utilized API access, indirect contamination was not a concern.
Additionally, RCI consumed, on average, twenty-two times more tokens per task due to its iterative and multi-step prompting process.
Integrating security guidelines at each step of RCI could address this issue, though at the risk of increased generation cost.
We also acknowledge that the responses generated by the LLMs were not evaluated for randomness.
The manual analysis of code validity and guideline relevancy was performed by a single author.
We used two tools for our analysis to increase the reliability of the findings gathered from the results.
Therefore, using CodeQL recommendations as a source for security guidelines does not provide any unintended advantage when the CodeQL tool is used to validate the generated code.

Additionally, as shown in Table IV, this approach took an average of 70.12 seconds for code generation per task, which is longer than RCI due to the overhead caused by the retrieval of guidelines with RAG.
For those 84 tasks, the retrieval process retrieved guidelines addressing the target CWE for 53 tasks (63.01%).
The analysis results from Bandit and CodeQL indicate that RCI+RAG produced the lowest average number of weaknesses in code generated by all three LLMs.
Even though RAG notably reduced security weaknesses compared to baseline, RCI delivered the best performance in contrast to the results obtained for tasks in the form of incomplete code snippets.
